title: Cyperus distans: How to Spot and Control Slender Cyperus in Rice
metaTitle: Cyperus distans in Rice: Slender Cyperus ID and Control
metaDescription: Cyperus distans, or slender cyperus, is a perennial sedge in lowland rice. Learn to spot its slender red spikelets and remove whole clumps for good.
excerpt: Cyperus distans, or slender cyperus, is a perennial sedge weed of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. It spreads by seed, and its clumps can live for more than one season. This page shows how to spot its slender, reddish spikelets and how to keep it out of your palay.

heroImage.alt: Slender cyperus (Cyperus distans), a sedge weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: R. O. Gardner, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family. Its English name is slender cyperus, a name that fits its thin, spreading spikelets. The PhilRice eDamuhan list gives no Filipino local name for it, so this page uses its scientific name, Cyperus distans. You will find it in both irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields.

It is a perennial, so a clump can stay alive from one season to the next. It spreads by seed. Each flowering stem drops seeds into the soil, and those seeds sprout when farmers prepare the field again. Since old clumps also survive between crops, you face both old plants and new seedlings each season. That is why removing whole clumps, and not just the tops, makes the biggest difference.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about Cyperus distans
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: Like other sedges, it has a solid, triangular stem with no nodes. The stems stand erect and feel smooth, and the three edges are easy to feel when you roll a stem between your fingers. Its leaves grow about as long as the stems. At the top, the flower head forms an open umbrella. Its slender spikelets spread outward, with a red or reddish brown color.

items: Smooth, erect stems with three edges and no joints along the length.
Leaves that grow about as long as the stems themselves.
An open, umbrella shaped flower head at the top of each stem.
Slender spikelets that spread outward, colored red or reddish brown.
Clumps that survive from last season, since this sedge is a perennial.

blocks.text:
Like most sedges, Cyperus distans competes with palay for light, water and fertilizer. Because it is a perennial, its clumps can stay in the field from one crop to the next. So the rice you plant may meet an old, established clump instead of a weak seedling.

When it flowers, its seeds add to the weed seed bank in your soil. Those seeds can also mix with harvested palay and lower the quality of seed you keep. Thick clumps give shelter to rats and insect pests near the rice hills too.

items: Dig out each clump with its base and roots instead of cutting the top, because a perennial clump can sprout again.
Remove plants before the red spikelets ripen and fall, since this sedge spreads by seed.
Clear clumps from bunds and field edges after harvest, so they do not survive to the next season.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold Cyperus distans down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Cyperus distans Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Cyperus distans?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Cyperus distans

items.q: What is the common name of Cyperus distans?
items.a: In English it goes by slender cyperus. The PhilRice eDamuhan list gives no Filipino local name for it, so this guide uses the scientific name. If you are not sure you have the right weed, look for slender, red or reddish brown spikelets that spread out from an umbrella shaped head on a three sided stem.

items.q: How do I control it in my rice field?
items.a: Use clean seed and keep the field well leveled with steady water. Next, dig out whole clumps by hand, base and roots included, before they flower. Clear the bunds after harvest so old clumps do not carry over. If you need a herbicide, choose one for sedges that fits the age of your rice, and follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Is slender cyperus harmful to rice?
items.a: Yes. Like other sedges, it competes with palay for light, water and fertilizer. Since it is a perennial, an old clump can keep taking those resources season after season. Its seeds also add to the weeds you will face next crop. Removing whole clumps early keeps the damage small and saves you work later.
